{{Short description|American statistician}}
'''Katherine Bennett Ensor''' is an American statistician specializing in numerous methods in [[computation]]al and [[statistical analysis]] of [[time series]] data, [[stochastic process]] modeling, and estimation to forecast issues in [[public health]], community [[informatics]], [[Computational finance#:~:text=Computational finance is a branch, realize financial models or systems.|computational finance]], and [[environmental statistics]].

Ensor is the Noah G. Harding Professor of Statistics and director of the Center for Computational Finance and Economic Systems at [[Rice University]]. From 2016–2022, she was director of the Kinder Institute Urban Data Platform, a data resource initiative for the [[Greater Houston]] area that includes the Texas Flood and COVID-19 registries. She is an executive team member for Houston Wastewater Epidemiology, a [[SARS-CoV-2]] wastewater monitoring initiative between Rice University, the Houston Health Department, Houston Public Works, and the City of Houston.<ref>{{Cite web|title=curriculum vitae|url=http://ensor.rice.edu/curriculum-vitae/}}</ref> In August 2022, Houston Wastewater Epidemiology was named a National Wastewater Surveillance System (NWSS) [[Center of excellence|Center of Excellence]] by the U.S. [[Centers for Disease Control and Prevention]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=CDC, National Wastewater Surveillance System, Centers of Excellence |date=21 May 2025 |url=https://www.cdc.gov/nwss/centersofexcellence.html }}</ref>

== Career and Research ==
Ensor's statistical and computational methods for the development of modeling frameworks pinpoint, track and forecast issues across a wide variety of fields.

Since the start of her academic career, a focus of her research has sought a deeper understanding of problems in energy,<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Raath|first1=Kim|last2=Ensor|first2=Katherine|date=23 June 2020|title=Time-varying wavelet-based applications for evaluating the water-energy nexus|journal=Frontiers in Energy Research|volume=8|article-number=118|doi= 10.3389/fenrg.2020.00118|doi-access=free |bibcode=2020FrER....8..118R }}</ref> quantitative finance<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Ensor|first1=Katherine|last2=Koev|first2=Ginger|date=25 July 2014|title=Computational finance: correlation, volatility, and markets|journal=WIREs Computational Statistics|volume=6|issue=5|pages=326–340|doi=10.1002/wics.1323|doi-access=free}}</ref><ref>{{Cite conference|last1=Kyj|first1=Lada|last2=Ostdiek|first2=Barbara|last3=Ensor|first3=Katherine|date=22 March 2009|title=Covariance estimation in dynamic portfolio optimization: a realized single factor model|journal=American Finance Association Annual Meeting|doi=10.2139/ssrn.1364642|ssrn=1364642 |doi-access=free}}</ref> and risk management.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Ensor|first1=Katherine|last2=Glynn|first2=Peter|date=1 April 2000|title=Simulating the maximum of a random walk|journal=Journal of Statistical Planning and Inference|volume=85|issue=1–2|pages=127–135 |doi=10.1016/S0378-3758(99)00075-0|doi-access=free}}</ref> In 2002, she collaborated with university and industry partners to establish the Center for Computational Finance and Economic Systems (CoFES). She has since continued to serve as the center's director and has developed numerous programs in graduate and undergraduate research and education.<ref>{{Cite web|title=cofes.rice.edu|url=https://cofes.rice.edu/}}</ref>

Ensor is widely known for her expertise in community analytics, which has grown through her career-long commitment to environmental and health-based research. Through collaborations with [[Academic discipline|cross-disciplinary groups]] of educators, scientists, engineers, and city and public health professionals, she has quantitatively assessed air quality and human exposure to environmental contaminants. The work has also included the discovery of a correlation between [[ozone]] and [[Myocardial infarction|heart attacks]], and of geographic patterns in severe [[asthma]] attacks in schoolchildren.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Ensor|first1=Katherine|last2=Raun|first2=Loren|last3=Persse|first3=David|date=2013-02-13|title=A case-crossover analysis of out-of-hospital cardiac arrest and air pollution|journal=Circulation|volume=127|issue=11|pages=1192–1199|doi=10.1161/CIRCULATIONAHA.113.000027|pmid=23406673|s2cid=173692|doi-access=free |bibcode=2013Circu.127.1192E }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Raun|first1=Loren|last2=Ensor|first2=Katherine|last3=Persse|first3=David|date=2014|title=Using community level strategies to reduce asthma attacks triggered by outdoor air pollution: a case crossover analysis|journal=Environmental Health|volume=13|issue=1|page=58 |doi=10.1186/1476-069X-13-58|pmid=25012280|pmc=4108967 |s2cid= |doi-access=free|bibcode=2014EnvHe..13...58R }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Raun|first1=Loren|last2=Jefferson|first2=Larry|last3=Persse|first3=David|last4=Ensor|first4=Katherine|date=August 2013|title=Geospatial analysis for targeting out-of-hospital cardiac arrest intervention|url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0749379713002729|journal=American Journal of Preventive Medicine|volume=45|issue=2|pages=137–142|doi=10.1016/j.amepre.2013.03.013|pmid=23867019|url-access=subscription}}</ref>

In May 2020, Ensor and collaborators at Rice University, the Houston Health Department, Houston Public Works, and the City of Houston, began conducting ongoing testing of the city's wastewater treatment system for the presence of SARS-CoV-2, the virus that causes [[COVID-19]].<ref>{{Cite medRxiv|last1=Stadler|first1=L.|last2=Ensor|first2=K.B.|last3=Clark|first3=J.R.|last4=Kalvapalle|first4=P.|last5=LaTurner|first5=Z.W.|last6=Mojica|first6=L.|last7=Terwilliger|first7=A.|last8=Zhuo|first8=Y.|last9=Ali|first9=P.|last10=Avadhanula|first10=V.|last11=Bertolusso|first11=R.|last12=Crosby|first12=T.|last13=Hernandez|first13=H.|last14=Hollstein|first14=M.|last15=Weesner|first15=K.|last16=Zong|first16=D.M.|last17=Persse|first17=D.|last18=Piedra|first18=P.A.|last19=Maresso|first19=A.W.|last20=Hopkins|first20=L.|date=2020-11-06|title=Wastewater Analysis of SARS-CoV-2 as a Predictive Metric of Positivity Rate for a Major Metropolis|medrxiv=10.1101/2020.11.04.20226191}}</ref>

The wastewater monitoring system has also been adapted to provide public health information on seasonal [[influenza]], the [[respiratory syncytial virus]] (RSV), [[mpox]], [[measles]], and up to 29 potential human [[pathogen]]s.<ref>{{Cite web|title=news and information/manuscripts|url=https://hou-wastewater-epi.org/news-and-information/manuscripts/}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Hopkins|first1=Loren|last2=Persse|first2=David|last3=Caton|first3=Kelsey|last4=Ensor|first4=Katherine|last5=Schneider|first5=Rebecca|last6=McCall|first6=Camille|last7=Stadler|first7=Lauren |date=10 January 2023|title=Citywide wastewater SARS-CoV-2 levels strongly correlated with multiple disease surveillance indicators and outcomes over three COVID-19 waves|journal=Science of the Total Environment|volume=855|article-number=158967|doi=10.1016/j.scitotenv.2022.158967|pmid=36162580|pmc=9507781 |bibcode=2023ScTEn.85558967H |doi-access=free}}</ref>

As director of the Kinder Institute Urban Data Platform from 2016–2022, Ensor investigated historical Houston flood event trends and [[Hurricane Harvey]] and on the health and housing impacts of the [[COVID-19 pandemic]] and [[COVID-19 vaccine]]s.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Callender|first1=Rashida|last2=Canales|first2=Joally|last3=Avendano|first3=Carolina|last4=Craft|first4=Elena|last5=Ensor|first5=Katherine|last6=Miranda|first6=Marie Lynn|date=November 2022|title=Economic and mental health impacts of multiple adverse events: Hurricane Harvey, other flooding events, and the COVID-19 pandemic|journal=Environmental Research|volume=124, Part 3|issue=Pt 3 |article-number=114020|doi=10.1016/j.envres.2022.114020|pmid=35948147|pmc=9357442 |bibcode=2022ER....21414020C |doi-access=free}}</ref> Additional studies have investigated mitigating risk and the affects climate change.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Texas Flood Registry, Measuring the Impacts of Extreme Weather and Planning for the Future |url=https://floodregistry.rice.edu/ }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Fagnant|first1=Carlynn|last2=Gori|first2=Avantika|last3=Sebastian|first3=Antonia|last4=Bedient|first4=Philip|last5=Ensor|first5=Katherine|date=1 September 2020|title=Characterizing spatiotemporal trends in extreme precipitation in Southeast Texas|journal=Natural Hazards|volume=104|issue=2 |pages=1597–1621|doi=10.1007/s11069-020-04235-x|doi-access=free|bibcode=2020NatHa.104.1597F }}</ref>

Ensor advises on computational and statistical analysis in science and engineering as chair of the National Academy of Science, Engineering, and Medicine (NASEM) committee on Frontiers of Statistics in Science and Engineering: 2035 and Beyond.<ref>{{Cite web |title=National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine Committee on Frontiers of Statistics in Science and Engineering: 2035 and Beyond |url=https://www.nationalacademies.org/our-work/frontiers-of-statistics-in-science-and-engineering-2035-and-beyond }}</ref> She is a member of the board of trustees for the National Science Foundation (NSF) Institute for Pure and Applied Mathematics (IPAM),<ref>{{Cite web |title=Institute for Pure and Applied Mathematics (IPAM), Board of Trustees |date=17 September 2022 |url=https://www.ipam.ucla.edu/people/board-of-trustees/ }}</ref> a member of the scientific review board for the Health Effects Institute (HEI),<ref>{{Cite web |title=Health Effects Institute (HEI), Scientific Review Board |url=https://www.healtheffects.org/about/review-committee }}</ref> and serves as chair of Section U (Statistics) for the American Association for the Advancement of Science (AAAS).<ref>{{Cite web |title=American Association for the Advancement of Science, Section U - Statistics |url=https://www.aaas.org/governance/section-u }}</ref>

From 2024 to 2025 Ensor was a representative director of the criteria committee on behalf of ASA for the Computer Science Academic Board (CSAB) – an organization within the Accreditation Board for Engineering and Technology (ABET).<ref>{{Cite web |title=Computer Science Academic Board (CSAB), Leadership |url=https://csab.org/about-us/#1589395269803-16039753-c2b9}}</ref> She was the 117th president of the [[American Statistical Association]]'s (ASA) board of directors (2021–2022)<ref>{{Cite web|title=magazine.amstat.org|work=Amstat News |date=July 2020 |url=https://magazine.amstat.org/blog/2020/07/01/katherine-ensor-elected-2022-asa-president/}}</ref> and vice president of ASA's board of directors from 2016 to 2018. She was a member of the [[National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine|National Academies of Sciences, Engineering and Medicine]] (NASEM) Committee on Applied and Theoretical Statistics (CATS) from 2015 to 2021.{{r|cv}}

Ensor earned bachelor's and master's degrees in mathematics from [[Arkansas State University]] in 1981 and 1982. She completed her Ph.D. in statistics in 1986 from [[Texas A&M University]];{{r|cv}} her dissertation, supervised by H. Joseph Newton, was ''Some Results in Autoregressive Modeling''.{{r|mgp}} She has been on the Rice faculty since 1987.{{r|cv}}
